metadata.case_name: WONG SUN CHEONG, SUING BY HIS NEXT FRIEND LEE YIN SHEUNG v. CHOI CHI KONG AND ANOTHER

plaintiff.occupation_before: delivery man at Kai Ming Food Shop

injuries.description: Severe head injury / traumatic brain injury
source: As a result of the collision, P sustained severe head injuries as is borne out by the agreed medical evidence.

Dr Choa and Dr Yu agreed that P had sustained a severe head injury as a result of the collision. There was loss of consciousness, prolonged post‑traumatic amnesia, skull fractures and multiple sites of intracranial bleeding requiring two emergency operations in the first two days to control.

injuries.description: Fractures on the left side of his skull
source: “Radiological investigations showed fractures on the left side of his skull, subarachnoid bleeding, subdural bleeding as well as contusion of the brain substance.”
injuries.icd_description: Fracture of vault of skull, unspecified

source: “Radiological investigations showed fractures on the left side of his skull, subarachnoid bleeding, subdural bleeding as well as contusion of the brain substance.”
“Radiological investigations showed fractures on the left side of his skull, subarachnoid bleeding, subdural bleeding as well as contusion of the brain substance.”
“Radiological investigations showed fractures on the left side of his skull, subarachnoid bleeding, subdural bleeding as well as contusion of the brain substance.”
“In May 2012, he was re‑admitted to QEH for his third operation, a cranioplasty to repair the skull defect with a metallic prosthesis.”
On physical examination of his head and neck and nervous system, their findings were as follows: "The craniectomy scar on the left side of his skull was noted."

injuries.description: Post‑traumatic epilepsy (status epilepticus in August 2012, commenced on phenytoin)
source: “In August 2012, while having lunch at home, he developed status epilepticus with refractory generalized epileptic seizures. He was admitted to Kwong Wah Hospital where the seizures were controlled with some difficulty. He needed to spend time in the intensive care unit where he was intubated. He was then started on the antiepileptic drug phenytoin which he continues to take. He has been seizure‑free since that one occasion.”
“It was also agreed that as a result of the severe head injury P had dysphasia (problem with language) and cognitive dysfunction and epilepsy.”
injuries.icd_description: Epilepsy due to injuries to the head

manifestations.description: Prolonged post‑traumatic amnesia estimated as over one month
Dysphasia (problem with language); impaired ability to express himself (often using the wrong words); impaired understanding of verbal communications
Cognitive dysfunction; scored 18/30 on mini mental state examination (mild to moderate dementia); naming difficulty; slowed comprehension
Epileptic seizures / status epilepticus (Aug 2012) treated and on ongoing antiepileptic medication (phenytoin)
Truncal ataxia; could not walk heel to toe; walked stably but with truncal ataxia; able to stand with feet together and eyes closed
Right leg mild spasticity with heightened reflexes
Not fully independent even inside the home; needs care and attention for the rest of his life
Permanent neurological deficits (as agreed by experts)
Permanent loss of earning capacity 100%; not employable in any capacity
not capable of managing his own legal and financial affairs and is not fully independent even inside the home

treatments_received: Emergency operation on day of admission to evacuate blood clots and to insert a ventricular drain
Further emergency operation the following day to evacuate more blood clots
Transfer to Kowloon Hospital for rehabilitation
Third operation (cranioplasty to repair the skull defect with a metallic prosthesis) in May 2012
Admission to intensive care unit and intubation for status epilepticus; started on antiepileptic drug phenytoin

losses.description: Severe head injury with skull fractures, intracranial bleeding and contusion of brain substance requiring multiple emergency operations and cranioplasty.
dysphasia (problem with language); impaired ability to express himself (often using the wrong words) as well as understanding of verbal communications
Cognitive dysfunction (MMSE 18/30; mild to moderate dementia), naming difficulty and slowed comprehension.
Not capable of managing his own legal and financial affairs and not fully independent even inside the home; needs care and attention for life.
Truncal ataxia; inability to walk heel to toe; gait impairment.
With P’s cognitive dysfunction, dysphasia, incontinence and impaired balance, P was not employable in any capacity; his permanent loss of earning capacity was 100%
